title: Curiosity Rover Finds “Sea of Polygons” on Martian Surface
gist: NASA's Curiosity rover, deployed to Gale Crater on Aug. 6, 2012, is still returning images 14 years later — the latest showing a vast field of honeycomb polygons in the Martian regolith. JPL project scientist Ashwin Vasavada says the team has measured the shapes and chemistry and hopes the data reveals how the features formed.

insights.claim: NASA deployed the Curiosity rover to explore Mars' Gale Crater on Aug. 6, 2012, and 14 years later the robot is still beaming back photos.
insights.speaker: Jake Currie
insights.so_what: Robotic hardware vastly outliving its mission window is the quiet economic case for nuclear-powered surface assets over short-duration landers.
insights.locator: On Aug. 6, 2012, NASA deployed the Curiosity rover

themes.theme: Sea of polygons in Martian regolith

insights.claim: Curiosity's latest images show striking honeycomb patterns in the Martian regolith stretching as far as the rover's camera can see, a landscape NASA staff describe as a 'sea of polygons.'
insights.speaker: Jake Currie
insights.so_what: Large-scale patterned ground is typically read as evidence of past wet/dry or freeze-thaw cycling — it feeds directly into the habitability case for Mars sample work.
insights.quote: We’ve seen a lot of fascinating landscapes through Curiosity’s eyes, but this sea of polygons took our breath away
insights.locator: The latest show striking honeycomb patterns

insights.claim: JPL project scientist Ashwin Vasavada said the team carefully measured the shapes and chemistry of the Martian honeycomb structures and is hopeful the data contains clues to how the features formed.
insights.speaker: Jake Currie
insights.so_what: Formation mechanism is still unresolved — the interpretation, not the imagery, is the pending catalyst.
insights.quote: We measured their shapes and chemistry carefully and are hopeful there are clues in the data as to how these features formed.
